entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Werferth, Bishop of Worcester from approximately 872 CE until his death in 915 CE, was a pivotal figure in the intellectual and ecclesiastical revival initiated by King Alfred the Great in late 9th-century Wessex. As one of the few scholars of his era fluent in Latin, Werferth played a crucial role in Alfred's ambitious program to restore learning and literacy in Anglo-Saxon England, a period often termed the Alfredian Renaissance. His significance lies primarily in his monumental translation of Pope Gregory the Great's *Dialogues* from Latin into Old English, a work that not only made foundational Christian hagiography accessible to a wider English-speaking audience but also significantly advanced the development of Old English prose as a literary and scholarly medium.

Werferth's translation of the *Dialogues*, completed sometime before 890 CE, was a direct response to King Alfred's lament regarding the widespread decline of Latin literacy among the clergy and educated elite. This effort was part of Alfred's broader strategy to translate 'certain books that are most necessary for all men to know' into the vernacular. Werferth's version of Gregory's work, which recounted the lives and miracles of Italian saints, including Benedict of Nursia, was not a mere word-for-word rendition but a nuanced adaptation, demonstrating a sophisticated command of both languages. Beyond his scholarly contributions, Werferth was a prominent ecclesiastical leader, serving as a witness to numerous charters and actively participating in the administration of the West Saxon kingdom, solidifying the Church's role in the intellectual and political landscape.
